newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton-Prices seen up in India, down in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Prices seen up in India, down in Pakistan.

text.p: Pakistani cotton prices are likely to slip on low demand next week, while Indian rates should rise after tumbling this week, dealers said on Thursday.

Karachi dealers said prices fell this week with spinners sidelined ahead of a relief package for the textile industry promised by Pakistan's new caretaker government. The government is expected to reduce duties on raw cotton and synthetic fibre imports to help the industry cope with a shortfall in domestic cotton output.
Pakistan's 1996/97 (July-June) cotton crop is now estimated at 9.2 to 9.5 million bales, below a target of 10 million and the 1995/96 crop of 9.96 million bales.
"The market is likely to come off further as spinners are likely to go for less expensive imported cotton and synthetic fibre after the package is unveiled," dealer Naseem Usman said.
On the kerb market NIAB-78 traded at 2,100 rupees ($52.21) per maund (37.32 kg), dealers said.
Karachi Cotton Association weekly cotton spot rates in rupees per maund - ($1 = 40.22 rupees)
In India, prices were hit last week by fresh arrivals and a drop in purchases by mills, dealers said. "Sluggish mill buying and rising new crop arrivals dragged prices lower," one said.
Even reports that the government had allowed the export of 15,000 tonnes of cotton yarn failed to cheer the market.
In spot deals Bengal-deshi slid to 890/915 rupees per maund from 915/940 rupees during the week.

Punjab saw-ginned moved down 40/50 rupees to 1,540/1,640 rupees per maund. Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) fell 700/800 rupees to 18,000/19,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg). Daily new crop arrivals in the Punjab region rose to 25,000/30,000 170-kg bales against the previous average of 10,000/15,000 bales.

"Sentiment remained subdued amid low physical enquiries from millers," one broker said. "Major millers kept on the sidelines expecting further price erosion while some millers were facing a financial crunch," he said.
"Even fresh purchases by state-owned agencies remained low which in turn aided a further slide, but these agencies may resume buying, looking at the sharp fall in prices," he said.
